title: Liver zones, the oxygen gradient, and C Y P two E one

segs.text: Section eighteen. Liver zones, the oxygen gradient, and C Y P two E one. Within the liver, a hepatotoxin often damages one zone and spares the others. The acinus view follows the blood from the vessels that bring it in, the hepatic artery and the portal vein, across to the central vein where it leaves. Zone one is closest to the inflow vessels. Zone three is closest to the central vein. Zone two lies between them.

The first reason for site-specific damage is the oxygen gradient. Blood enters zone one fairly well oxygenated. As it flows past the hepatocytes, they take oxygen out of it, so by the time it reaches the central vein it is relatively hypoxic. Zone one has the most oxygen and zone three the least. If the enzymes that bioactivate a compound need oxygen to work, the high oxygen in zone one helps them. The hepatotoxic metabolite is made there, and zone one is damaged. Relatively high oxygen content in zone one was the keyed answer to her poll. Reversing the gradient is a trap.

The second reason is where the enzymes are. Zone one has many phase two enzymes. Zone three has some P four fifties, and C Y P two E one is expressed more there than in zone one. In overdose, acetaminophen is bioactivated to N A P Q I by C Y P two E one. Because C Y P two E one is highest in zone three, N A P Q I is made in zone three, and a biopsy shows hepatocyte death in zone three. She said, most of our metabolizing enzymes are not homogeneously expressed across the entire liver.

Two other options on that poll are false. Homogenous expression of P four fifties across the zones is false, and C Y P two E one is the counterexample. Zone two having few Kupffer cells is also false. Kupffer cells move all over the liver, in every zone, so they cannot explain one zone being spared. The two reasons for site-specific liver damage are the oxygen gradient across the zones, and the uneven expression of metabolizing enzymes such as the C Y P four fifties.
